utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Tecla Benjamin, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon; and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber greets all present, the Prosecution, the Defence, and the accused. We shall finish this week with two witnesses. We are going to start immediately. If there are not any preliminaries, we are going to bring the first witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I'm going to ask you whether you hear the interpreters, first of all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You're going to give me your name and your family name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Drago Pesa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 25 September 1954.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Travnik municipality, in the village of Podovi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm unemployed. I was a mining technician before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the place where I was born.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You have been asked to testify on behalf of the Prosecution. First of all, you are going to read the text that Madam Usher is going to show to you. Please read it in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have already told you, the Prosecution has invited you to appear as a witness. You are a witness of the Prosecution. During your testimony, you are going to be asked to answer questions put to you by the Prosecution, who are sitting on your right-hand side. After these questions, the Defence counsel, who are sitting on your left, will have the right to ask you questions. There are six of them, but only two will be asking questions. And the three Judges, who are sitting in front of you, can also ask you questions to clarify some things. When you answer the questions, try to be as complete as possible in your answers. If you don't understand a question, the person who has put the question may be asked to rephrase it. Have you understood that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution for their examination-in-chief. Let's be clear. We have two witnesses today. You have the floor, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, before we begin, I just wish to draw to your attention that on the trial schedule, I was schedule to do this in 0.5 of an hour, and I wish to inform the Trial Chamber that I may just need a little more time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pesa.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You indicated to the President of the Trial Chamber that you were born in Podovi in the municipality of Travnik. Could you tell the Trial Chamber at that time what was the ethnic composition of Podovi.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: At that time, the village was inhabited predominantly by Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you give us a figure breakdown?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: There were about 300 Croats and a lot more Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you tell the Trial Chamber in that period in time what was the relationship basically between the villagers.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: The relationship between Croats and Muslims, that is, Bosniaks, as far as the local population is concerned, the relationship was very concrete. There were some minor misunderstandings, but those would be overcome by reaching agreements. And there were no major problems, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pesa, could you come a little closer to the mic, please. Could you speak a little closer in the mic. Thank you. Are you married?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes. I have eight -- that is, nine children. I had nine children. Eight are still living, and one son of mine was executed by shooting, so he died.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what year, in what year he died.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: In 1993. On the 8th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1992, Witness, war broke out in Bosnia. Could you tell us whether the onset of the war, if there was an invasion of foreigners in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes. They started arriving in early 1992 in an organised manner. They arrived in vans and minibuses. Most of them were from Arabic countries, as a matter of fact. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you refer to these foreigners by any particular name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: We had market days when our produce was sold in Mehurici. Bosniaks, Muslims would tell us that those people who had arrived originated from Arabic countries. They were different in the way they behaved, their culture was different, and they differed in their appearances. They were different from the local Bosnian-Herzegovinian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. But do you know if they were described by a particular name? Do you know? Were they called by a particular name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: They were for the most part Arabs, and I didn't know their names. They wore the typical clothes worn in Arab countries. They wore headpieces around their heads. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay, Witness, yes, you can describe them, but this group of people, do you know if they were called by a particular name? Were they given a name? Not individual persons, but the group. Was the group described?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: They were called something like Mujahedini, Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pesa, were you a member of any army at any time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the Territorial Defence, which comprised of both Croats and Bosniaks, that is, Muslims. That was in 1992 up to February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And after 1993, were you a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: No. Those were my last days in the Territorial Defence, when my colleagues --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. In line 11, it seems that in her question my learned friend mentioned the JNA, and the witness has never said that he was in the JNA in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President. In fact, I meant to ask him if he was ever a member of the JNA. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Pesa, were you a member of any other army in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Were you a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Once we were expelled, I joined HVO units in Nova Bila. And before that, I served in the army, the ex-Yugoslav army, in the years 1973 and 1974.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pesa, could you tell this Trial Chamber in the spring of 1993, if you can recall, if there was anything significant to you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. From the village of Miletici, my mother's brothers and their children, which constitute my close family -- a terrible slaughter took place in Miletici. Croats were slaughtered there. Franjo Pavlovic was slaughtered together with Tihomir Pavlovic, Ante Kozina, Stipo Pavlovic. Their heads were cut off. They were put on a plate. Their hearts were taken out. And crosses were drawn on their foreheads and the lower part -- I don't know what to call it -- their lower body organs were cut off and put into their mouth. Those people who were still alive had to drink the blood of their children. And when they started putting them away - let me just add this - they put them on buses and they started transporting them towards Mehurici. However, close to the tunnel, when they were still on the buses, the driver was ordered to -- to push the bus down the precipice beneath the tunnel. However, the driver refused to do that. His conscience, I suppose, would not allow him to do that. I'm sorry, I am very moved. I'm sorry for sounding like this. The driver had received an order to drive them to Poljanice to a cowshed. They were supposed to be burnt down in that cowshed. I don't want to mention this person's name. If I have to, I can mention his name. I can tell you who this person was. This person is still alive. I know him very well. I thought well of him. So this didn't happen. They drove them to a school and in that school --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay, Witness, thank you. That was quite helpful. Thanks. But we need to move on. And could you describe for me the prevailing mood in Bosnia and in particular your village in and around May of 1993.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: I've just said that. If somebody in the village next to you would live through all that, would that meet with the compassion of their co-villagers? If you saw all these atrocities, I don't think that anybody on this earth might feel comfortable after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. In just one word, would you describe that around May of 1993 the mood would be tense? Would I be correct in asking that question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Was the presence of soldiers visible on the streets in that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: My house is close to the main road which connects all of these villages. Every morning I would see them doing their morning training. They would be shouting out slogans, " Allah-U-Ekber," "Tekbir," and they were also saying, "This is going to be a Turkish land."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You tell us "they." Could you tell us what you mean when you say "they." Who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Most of them wore green bandannas on their heads. And those from Arabic countries sported long beards. They had long knives and they also had automatic and semiautomatic rifles and similar kinds of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pesa, can you recount for the Trial Chamber the events that took place on the 7th of June, 1993, as you can remember.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: I am a Croat, but I would like to receive the interpretation in Croatian when it comes to months. On the 5th of -- on the 7th of June, we didn't know what was going on. We were already at the mercy of events, and everybody had to manage as they could. Since my family is very numerous, I had many kums among Bosniaks, Muslims. A lot of Muslims were godparents to my children, and I didn't think that anything like that could ever happen to us, because we relied on each other. And if I had something, my neighbours could rely on having the same thing. So I could never imagine that something like that could ever happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us, then, now that you have given us the preamble, what transpired on the 7th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to tell you about the 7th of June, 1993. I thought there was no need for me to go anywhere. I thought I could stay. However, when I got up that morning, a man came up to my house. I had never seen him before. He asked me what my ethnic background was. I said I was a Croat. And then he told me, "You have this much time to leave your house." And then I told him, "What did I ever do to you?" However, my wife and my children were in a state of panic. And then I said, "Did I ever do anything bad? Please don't touch my children. Kill me rather than them." And he said, "No, we are not going to kill you. We're just giving you a deadline to leave your house." But those people with green bandannas, I believe that they were members of the Muslim forces in cooperation with these Arab people from the Arabic countries. They were standing on the side, and they supervised this man who came up to my house. Then I said to my wife and my children, "Go and -- go and collect some of your things and just flee, just run away." I had a young boy that I had to carry. We were walking by a stream from the Malinska [phoen] cave.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Did you leave the house? Did you leave the house?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. So could you tell us where you went.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: We went towards Postinje, and then via Postinje we went towards Maljine.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly who was in the group that was en route to Maljine.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: The villagers of Podovi and my family. When we arrived in Podovi, it was a living hell out there. We were enclosed from all sides. Those who managed to escape saved their lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: From Maljine, did you go to any other village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: We went towards Krpeljici. But then when the late Sreco Bobas said that we should go towards Borovi -- this is where my relative was killed. I can't remember his name. He had a licence to carry a pistol. They found this pistol on him, and that's why they killed him. Still Sreco told us that we should go towards Borovi, and I told him, "Sreco, this is an open space. There are sniper shooters around. They will kill us." No sooner did I say that, the late Sreco fell on the ground, and then I said, "Let's go down to the stream and continue along the stream in order to get to Krpeljici."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: On your way to Krpeljici, could you describe for the Trial Chamber what happened.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Well, you see, we came across obstacles that you had to be very careful. You couldn't go through open spaces that provided no cover, but you had to take shelter in the bushes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Why did you have to take shelter in the bushes? What -- cover from what? Why did you have to take shelter in the bushes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Cover from attack, because I was with my family and I wanted to save them. But we managed to pass through, all of us, except for this son of mine who remained a captive, as well as my mother and father. But afterwards, we joined this brother of mine and we managed to reach Krpeljici eventually.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So it is your evidence to this Chamber that on your way to Krpeljici you were in the line of fire? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Oh, yes, indeed. It was horrific. It was as if you were in hell.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did anything in particular occur while you were in the line of fine? Did you see anything happening to anybody?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: There were people killed. But I personally, I couldn't recognise those people because my main concern was to save my family.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. That's understandable. Now, when you got to Krpeljici, tell us what happened. Did you stay in Krpeljici or did you move on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: No. We moved on towards Nova Bila. However, we were met there, but again we were going through the bushes to reach Nova Bila, which was held by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In Nova Bila, were you able to find out any information at all about any members of your family, while you were in Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived there - that was the next day - Pavo Barac had escaped from an execution site, as well as Puselja -- I can't recall his first name. He is now in America. His left shoulder had such a hole in it that you could put a cup in. Then Marijan Bobas, who died recently; and Ljuban Puselja; and Vlado Puselja, who escaped from the execution site. And when Pavo Puselja came to Nova Bila, I was already in the HVO by then in Nova Bila. My superior told me, "Drago, go to the hospital down there. I won't tell you anything in advance. You'll learn everything over there." When I arrived there, Pavo was absolutely out of his mind and he said, "Drago, I escaped execution, and I saw your Tihomir and the others, unarmed men who had surrendered because they never imagined that anything like that could happen and that my Tihomir and the other young men -- they were fine young men -- they were all shot dead .

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Upon hearing this -- this bit of news with respect to your son, did anything personally happen to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes. At the moment when I heard that -- before that, I had dark hair, and then overnight all my hair went white. And from that time, I've had an ulcer. I was hospitalised for 21 or 22 days, and from that time on I have never recovered. And to this very day I still feel the same pain.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, would the Court allow the witness to have some water, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, you can have some water at this point in time, if you like. Could you tell the Court -- there came a time, Witness, when you were released from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: We were expelled on the 8th of June. I believe that was in mid-July or maybe the end of July or even the beginning of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: I went to stay with some relatives in Nova Bila, those who had survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber why you didn't go back to your own home.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Why I didn't go home? Who would go back in such a situation, when all this had happened? I think it was better in hell.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you may take your time now, but could you tell us if you ever found or if the body of your son was ever found.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes. I received it in an exchange. This was in 1994, January or February, something like that, in 1994, the beginning of January or February, when they told us that they had received seven corpses in an exchange from the Muslim Bosniak authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Do you recall where you had to collect your son?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes. We went to an area known as Prahulje, near Nova Bila, and they let us see those corpses to see whether we could recognise members of our families or relatives or children.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Were you able to identify your son?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you describe for this Trial Chamber what you saw when you saw your son.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: When we were identifying these bodies, they were in nylon plastic bags. As they had been taken out of the ground, they were extremely muddy. We unzipped the bag, tore open the nylon, and when I looked, the colour of the hair, the body was still in relatively good condition so I could recognise him. And as my son had served the army in Dolac, he had completed his service and he was wearing military boots.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, may I interrupt here. Could you tell the Trial Chamber if the son who was in the army, is that the deceased son you're speaking of or is that somebody else, the one who was in the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: No, he wasn't in the army, but he was wearing the boots of my older son. They had exchanged their footwear. However, when we took those boots off his feet -- and this woman who was overseeing this, she said, "Pesa Miomir." And I said, "Madam, I apologise, it's Pesa Marinko." But on the boots, on the inside of the boots there was written "Pesa Marinko," so I knew immediately the boots were of my older son. And I continued looking, and I washed the boots a little to be able to read more easily the first and last name of the owner of the boots. And so we came to the conclusion that that was indeed my child. However, later on when we took him out of the bag, his head was facing towards the right, his hands were tied with wire, as well as his legs. These are so moving facts, and I do apologise. The bullet had entered his forehead, and there was another entry wound in the chest, and the exit wound was larger. The entry wound was about 1 centimetre in diameter, and the exit wound was twice that size.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And were you able to identify the other bodies that were with your son's body?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Well, you see, when you have a child in that situation, you focus everything and your whole attention on the child. Just then I didn't really pay much attention to the others, once I had found my own son and saw him in that state with his hands tied, his legs tied. Your brain or your memory, your mind focuses on that child of yours, to identify him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay, Witness. Thank you very, very much. That was very good. But I'd just like to know, with your son, not being physical identification, but could you tell us in terms of numbers how many other bodies did you see?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: I also saw Balta Mate's wife; Ljubica Ceko; Mijo Tavic. I'm sorry, I think there were four or five or six others there, but two bodies were not identified. And it said "NN," name unknown. And those who were with my son, I knew them, because they were recognised by members of their family, their relatives or -- or so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And finally, could you tell the Trial Chamber if you were given the opportunity to dispose of your son.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes. I buried him there at Prahulje. There's a morgue right next to the cemetery, about 100 metres away. And you had to do this at night, because the Muslim and Bosniak forces had targets that they shot at, both during daytime and during the night. But all the burials took place during the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber presently how you feel and how you're coping at this moment from the effects of your experience.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: I would just like to add that during the night we would bury the dead because there was shelling. And now I'll answer your last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: You see, I would like to underline that this was a stressful event, but I have other children and I would like to bring up those children as good and honest human beings with integrity to treat everyone well regardless, because God said "forgive others so that you may be forgiven." And that is my motto; it always has been, regardless of everything. And I have children who are still friends with Muslims and Serbs. I have told my children, "You mustn't nurture hatred towards anyone." And the fact that such an evil has been done to me, I will cope with that, my suffering, my pain. But I don't want you to feel that. I have eight children, wonderful children.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Believe me. They have Muslim colleagues and friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Pesa, you are -- will now have to answer some questions put to you by Defence counsel. I would like to ask you two points of clarification only. They don't have to do with the very painful facts that you have just described to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said at the very beginning that when you saw the Muslims coming from Arab countries arriving, they appeared to be organised. That is what you said. What prompted you to say that? These foreign Muslims who arrived, what prompted you to say they were organised? And if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: I was in the Territorial Defence in Mehurici, which means I was in the communications centre in the TO, so I had communication with those people. And they told me, "Our brothers are coming to our assistance. Our brothers from the Islamic countries, to assist us in our war operations." However, that made me feel uncomfortable, because I thought to myself, If we are all from Bosnia and Herzegovina, I never favoured that damned war. Why should we kill each other? We had no reason to do that. And they held the third floor of the elementary school. I went to that school, and I graduated from that school and I know it like my own home. And they said to me the following: "They don't know who is a Serb or a Croat. They are simply fighting against Christianity. They are against Christianity." They don't care whether you're a Serb or a Croat. They only treated Muslims and Bosniaks as human beings. And four or five of these vans would come, full of them. If I may add: I had a little boy. He was small. And he killed a snake. It was a coffee bar. And then because this little boy had killed the snake, he was threatened with a knife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question, which will refer you to the painful event that you described a moment ago, has to do with the exchange when you were able to collect the body of your body -- of your son. I'm sorry. You said there were people engaged in this exchange. And those people who were there, to the best of your knowledge, who were they, the people who facilitated the delivery of your son's body?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: I don't know how to put it. It was a kind of cooperation, an exchange between the HVO and the Bosniak Muslim representatives or military representatives, people who were responsible for the exchange of the living or the dead or those killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will turn again towards the Defence. Has Defence counsel any questions for this witness, taking into account, of course, his condition, being the father of a victim. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pesa.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic, and I wish to express my condolences for having lost your son, but I will ask you to answer a few questions.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes, do. Do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that up until February 1993 you were in the Territorial Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was then that certain tensions increased between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO, and so you thought it was best to leave the TO.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: That was the advice I got from my well-intentioned Bosniak Muslim neighbours. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that, guard duty started to be organised in your village and you joined the HVO and took part in organising those guards; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from our learned colleagues and the President, you told us how these foreign fighters came to your area. Tell me, is it true that those foreigners spoke a language that you couldn't understand?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Arabic language.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also testified that they passed by your house and did physical exercises, chanting certain words. They were speaking Arabic, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes. I have to explain a little -- Only those who wore those green bandannas, who were wearing those Arabic clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But let me ask you briefly: You speak about the killing of your neighbours in Miletici. When that happened, you were not in Miletici, were you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: I wasn't, but I was told all this by one of the persons who escaped, and that is Bozo Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also never attended the identification of those bodies from Miletici.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes, I did, when they were being buried up there, between Susanj, and there's a cemetery that exists, and there are photographs. And the priest had the photographs, and his name was Pero Karajica, I think. I'm not quite sure. But I think that is how it was. He was in possession of all these photographs, the photographs of the misdeeds that were committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Later on you saw those photographs.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes, those photographs still exist to this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what you told Their Honours about the appearance of those bodies was based on what you saw on the photographs; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO PESA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does the other Defence team have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does the Prosecution have any re-examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't have any re-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Pesa, your testimony is over. The Chamber fully appreciates the effort you had to make to be able to testify about those very painful memories, and we thank you for making your contribution to the establishment of the truth within the framework of this case, and we wish you a safe return home. I'm going to ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, and good luck to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still have another half hour before the break. Perhaps we can begin with the next witness. Can we bring him in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Can you hear the interpretation, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been invited by the Prosecution to testify. I would like to hear your first name and your last name. Can you please say that for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to greet all present. My name is Vinko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When were you born and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 15th of October, 1965.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Cukle, Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a shop assistant, a tradesman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where do you currently reside ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I currently reside in Nova Bila, Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been invited to give your testimony. For that reason, we shall ask you to take a solemn declaration. Please read the text in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have already told you, the Prosecution thought that it would be useful for the establishment of the truth if you came and gave your testimony. You are first going to answer the questions put to you by the Prosecution, who are seated on your right. After those questions, the Defence counsel representing the accused, who are seated on your left, can also ask you questions. The three Judges, who are sitting in front of you, can also ask you questions if they deem it necessary to clarify some things or if they think that it would be necessary to establish the truth. While answering, try to give as complete answers as possible. If you do not understand a question, you can always ask the person who has put the question to repeat it or to rephrase it. We are going to begin. Your -- the beginning of your testimony will take 25 minutes. Then we shall have a break. And we will continue at five minutes to 11.00. I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution, who are going to start their examination-in-chief. Prosecution, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tadic. You indicated to the Trial Chamber that you were born in Cukle in the municipality of Travnik. And could you kindly tell the Trial Chamber or give the Trial Chamber an idea of the -- a breakdown of the ethnic composition of Cukle. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: As far as Cukle is concerned, there were 70 per cent Croats and some 30 per cent were Muslims, that is, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you assist the Trial Chamber with what was the relationship, the relationship that existed between the villagers of Cukle.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: The relationship between the local population was good up to 1993, when this conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, were you ever a member of the JNA? And if so, could you tell the Trial Chamber the length of period that you served. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: I was in the JNA from 1985 for the next 13 months. I served in Belgrade, and I was a member of Tito's Guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Were you -- did you serve in any other capacity, military capacity?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Were you a member -- were you ever a member of the Home Guards in Cukle?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: When it comes to being a member of Home Guards, before the 6th of June, when I was captured, 20 days prior to that the locals started organising themselves into the so-called village guards. People were already afraid, and there was a feeling of uncertainty among the people. However, we did not carry any arms. It was just to give us a feeling that something was happening, that something was being done.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: On the morning of the 6th of June, 1993, could you tell the Trial Chamber where you were.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of June, 1993, I was on the slopes of Mount Vlasic. To be more precise, I was in Konjska. This is where sheep were and nomads guarded sheep there and they had their huts where they stayed during the summer, while they were looking after the sheep.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And whilst there, did you hear anything? Did you observe anything?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: Before that, on Saturday -- the day when I was captured was Sunday. So on Saturday I set out from Cukle with my late father, because my brother, his sister and their -- his wife and their four children had already been up there with the sheep. We came up there, and on the road from Cukle to Konjska we could already hear shots from the sector of Mount Vlasic and from the sector of Mehurici and from the sector of Stari Travnik. We didn't know what was going on. When we arrived up there, we found some women and children there and some shepherds, who were there together with my brother and his family. And then they told us that allegedly conflicts had already started in Travnik and that some forces were firing from the sector of Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were approached at your shack? Did anybody approach you? And could you tell us what transpired as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: On Saturday, we arrived there late in the afternoon. We spent the night up there. And then in the morning, sometime between 6.00 and 7.00, at dawn, my father got up earlier than anybody else. He was outside. We were still not awake. We were in one shack: My brother, myself, my brother's wife, and his children. There was Nikola Volic and his wife and his son. We could hear some sort of noise coming from outside. We got up to see what was going on. As we looked out, we could hear the noise, and my father told me, "They are asking us to surrender. They're saying that we are captured." We didn't know what was going on, because we hadn't seen any army. There were no positions of any sort up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You have told this Trial Chamber that "they" had said, "We are captured." Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what do you mean by "they," who you mean by "they," who are you referring to as "they."

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: As the situation developed, we found out what this was all about. First some five or six young men appeared wearing military uniforms. On the left arms, they had green bands. They were quite angry, and they wanted to gather all of us from our shacks. And the number of people who were approaching the shacks increased with time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, at that time, did it appear to you if there was any particular person in charge? Was this ...?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: During the course of events, as I was being captured, as we were all being arrested, only a few children remained in the shacks. They were very young, these children. And a man approached me, a man whom they referred to as Hadzija. He held a bomb, a grenade in his hand. He approached me. He wanted to hit me. I managed to avoid that, and then they gathered us all and started taking us downhill towards Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, these men that you said, who guarded you and started to take you on to Mehurici, would you be able to describe for the Court in detail how they were dressed and what they looked like physically, briefly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: There were some 13 or 14 of them altogether. They all wore military uniforms, camouflage uniforms. They were armed. They carried rifles of all kinds, different models. And I noticed two soldiers who also had backpacks with tromblons in them. And on the left arms, they had dark green bands.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Were you able to notice whether these bands had any inscriptions on them, or were they just plain armbands?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: They had oval green insignia bearing the word "MOS." And they had a crescent and a star. They had an oval patch. I don't know whether all of them had them, but I noticed that a few soldiers had the oval patches with a star and a crescent.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I'd be grateful if the witness can be shown Exhibit P4.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you assist the Court whether or not with the description that you have given us, if you are able to identify any of those armbands or the insignias on the armbands that you just related to the Court.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: It looked like the patch under number 9, only the patch that I saw had a star above the crescent and below the crescent there was the word "MOS." And it was turned differently, upside down.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, could the document be marked and tendered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can he be shown a hard copy of this document to be able to put his initial on it. Do you have a hard copy of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this particular document has already been tendered as Exhibit P4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, at -- so in this case, the transcript will be enough and it will say that the witness has recognised the patch under number 9. So we can admit this into evidence -- we can admit -- we are going to be satisfied with the fact that the witness has visually recognised on the screen a patch which is not quite identical to the one that he saw. He has told us that there were other elements on the patch that he saw on that day, elements different to the one that he has seen on the screen. Witness, we are talking about the patch number 9. Did you see the 7th Muslim Brigade being mentioned on the patch that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it didn't say "The 7th Muslim Brigade." The only thing that I saw was "MOS" written in white; however, it was turned upside down. The crescent and the star were at the bottom, and beneath those two there was the word "MOS" in white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Proceed, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This exercise was just basically for clarification of the badge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, you told us previously that you were instructed by a particular individual to move on towards Mehurici. Did you follow the order? Did you comply with the order?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: The orders that were issued from the moment we were captured were issued by the person they called Hadzija. I don't know his first name or his last name; I only know that they referred to him as Hadzija. From the very first moment, they wanted us to gather all the sheep in one place and they wanted the sheep to be taken downhill to Mehurici, together with us. This was not possible. The attempt failed. They were in a rush. They gave up, and then they decided just to take us, the women, and children, and the men that they had captured. The terrain was very difficult to negotiate, and we found it very, very difficult to go downhill.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: When you finally arrived at Mehurici, could you tell the Trial Chamber where did you go to and if the group were still intact or if the group was broken. Could you explain to us what happened on your arrival at Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: We were walking all of us together. They were on the two flanks of the group. They escorted us. Just before we arrived in Mehurici, when we had already descended from Mount Vlasic, we arrived as far as the village called Poljanice. We noticed a large number of soldiers who were heavily armed. Some of them wore military uniforms; some of them wore civilian clothes. They were heavily armed. According to my estimate, they were over 100 troops who were ready to start moving. They started cursing us as we were passing by them, escorted by the troops that had captured us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And you got to Mehurici. And where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: As we arrived in Mehurici, we were taken to the primary school there. They put us on the ground floor in the sports hall. We stayed there for some hour or hour and a half, and then we were separated; the men were separated from the women and the children.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Where did the women and children stay?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: The women and the children stayed in the sports hall, and we were taken some 100 or 150 metres away from the school to a concrete shed. There was a number of concrete sheds there. This used to be a forger's workshop. And they put us there. There was a concrete floor. There was some two or three wooden benches. So this seems to be an old blacksmith's workshop.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us the measurement of the room. Could you give us a description of the measurement of the room.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: The room was 3 by 3. It was very dark. There was just one little round opening that was covered with some pieces of cloth. I believe that it served as ventilation. It was a small room, 3 by 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: How many -- could you tell the Trial Chamber how many members were in your group. How many people were in your group?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you the exact figure, but there were over 10 of us, between 10 and 13. I can tell you the names of the people who were there at the beginning. And then some others joined us later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you assist us with the names, please.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: I'll try. The first was my brother, Jozo Tadic; then Nikola Volic; Dragan Volic; Frano Volic; his son, whose name was also Frano; his son Mladen Volic; Ferdo Tadic, my brother; Mato Tadic, my father; Mijo Jelovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think since we are very close to the break this might be a convenient time for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Witness, we're going to break for 25 minutes. This will allow the technicians to change the tape. We shall resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are going to continue with the examination. Madam Benjamin, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, at the time of the break, you were in the process of describing the room where you were, in which you said that it was a room in a blacksmith's shop, or it was a blacksmith's shop. Could you please describe for the Trial Chamber this room; its measurement, you know, its physical appearance, please.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: The room was roughly 3 metres by 3. On the floor was concrete. There were three wooden benches on the sides, and at the back there was an opening, a round opening, circular in shape, of some 30 centimetres in diameter, which used to be used for ventilation purposes and it was blocked up with rags. So it was totally dark. And there was a wooden door.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it please it is Court now, I would wish to show the witness some pictures, which is my intention to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, on your screen you will see the first picture, which at the top right-hand corner says "0124-08187." Could you indicate to the Trial Chamber if you recognise this picture.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: That is a series of sheds. There were five or six such sheds attached to one another, and roughly, that would be the door to the room that we were held in, where these barrels are to the side. There were some benches where the guards used to sit who were guarding us and who were on duty there. And across the way, there was a house with a four-cornered roof, a civilian building, and they would gather in the yard in front of that house. They would shout all kinds of insults and they would provoke us. But this was on the other side of the road to the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could we have the second picture, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you do the same with this picture for us. Could you tell us if you can identify this picture.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: As for the interior of this room, I see a window there and some things there. In those days, it was completely empty. And as I was saying, there were about -- there were three wooden benches, but I don't remember there being any window. There was just a round hole that was left there from some sort of old ventilation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: When you say "a round hole," you mean an opening of some sort? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could we move on to picture number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And this, I believe, can you help us with what appears to be the interior. Does this look familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: It is an interior, but I see there now it seems to be with flooring, et cetera. But in those days it was completely empty. There was nothing inside. And there was just concrete on the floor. And where this window is now, that would roughly be the position of that ventilation opening which was blocked up, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you assist us with -- as you said earlier on, that door was the entrance door. Could you assist us if this is that very entrance door that you first described in the first picture.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I don't remember what the door looked like, what colour it was. But I can claim with certainty that there was a wooden door. It was just put together very roughly. Now, what colour they were, whether it was this door, I don't remember, but there was a wooden door. That, I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Next one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And this picture, 0124-8191, does that look as you have been describing? Does that look ...?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: So that would be this line of sheds, a row of sheds. And in one of them we were held. Here at the corner, where you see the beginning of this metal fence, this area behind the metal fence would be the area that they would lead us through to take us for some sort of interrogation. There was a building there owned by the Sebesic company. And there was a restaurant there, and they took us there for interrogation. And after a while, they would take us to the toilet there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And finally, 0124-8192. Could you help us with the location of this. At what -- what direction is this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: We can see this row of sheds. This is the macadam road that led to the cattle market. And where you see the man standing, that is the direction leading towards the school, towards the centre of Mehurici. And you can see a bit of the building where that restaurant used to be, Ugar. As for this old building next to the Ugar restaurant, they would take us to this old building, to the toilet there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Before we tend the same into evidence, could you tell this Trial Chamber why you would want to tell us that you are absolutely sure that these pictures that you have described are, in fact, that particular blacksmith shop that you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: Because -- I can claim 100 per cent because I used to come there before, when there was a blacksmith shop there, before the war, before the conflict. I would come there often to Mehurici and I would go to the cattle market there. And this -- in this old building, on the front side, there's an asphalt road, and there was a registry there, registry offices there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, may these pictures be tendered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are going to follow a certain order, because there may otherwise be some difficulties. Let us first take the last photograph, 1892. Witness, on the photograph 1892 that you have in front of you, there are three doors. As you were -- when you were detained there, which door did you use? The central door, the one to the left, or the one to the right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We entered through the central door, the door in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we can infer that you were held in the room behind that door; that is where you were detained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were told that to the right, where we see the gentleman standing, that there was a restaurant and that they went to the toilet in the building that we see the wall painted in white. Is that where you went to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think they took us here to this old building. But in view of the fear we were in, I am not quite sure whether it was this big building or the old building, but one of the two. But it is more probable that it was in this old building that we were taken to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see that building on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can see this side of it, to the right of these sheds. This old building there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we are going to give an exhibit number to this photograph. Will you please mark on the photograph your full name and today's date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And today's date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please show this document to the Prosecution; to the Defence counsel, please; the accused; the Chamber is going to look at the document too. Mr. Registrar, can I have a final exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P42. Now we're going to go on to the preceding photograph. Could the Prosecution show us the photograph on the monitor, please. So this is photograph ending with the numbers 91. And the witness told us that he took the door we saw there to enter the small yard and to be taken for interrogation. There was a kind of yard with a line there and that you took this door.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't take this door. We came out of the door between the barrels. Behind the fence, there was a small gate, and we passed through it to go for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. He's telling us that he took the door in the middle, between the barrels. They came out of that door. Then they took a small gate behind the fence to go to the place of the interrogation, which was in the restaurant. Is that right? Is that where you were interrogated? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The photograph you're looking at and that you have a copy of, will you please sign your name and put today's date on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Show the photograph, please, to the Prosecution, to Defence counsel, please, to the accused, to the Judges. Can I have an exhibit number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P43. Prosecution, will you please show us on the video the next photograph, ending with the number 90. When examined by the Prosecution, the witness was not able to tell us whether this was indeed the door which he saw at the time. Witness, the photograph that you're looking at now, could it correspond to the central door and the room in which you were detained? If you don't know, tell us. Say no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is certainly the same room, but I must repeat: I cannot claim with certainty that that was the same door. I know that it was a wooden door, but this photograph shows the interior of that room. Now, whether that was the same door or not, I can't remember. But there was a wooden door; I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the room, you can't tell us either whether that was the room in which you were detained=?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the room, the interior of the room, it was identical to this one. There was a concrete floor. You can see here some sort of covering. But in those days there was nothing; there were just three wooden benches inside. So that is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So please write your name and today's date on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we have a new exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next photograph, please; 89, ending with the number 89. Witness, this photograph shows a room. And you told us that to the best of your memory there was an opening that does not correspond to this window and that you couldn't tell us whether this was the room in which you were detained; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the interior of the room, it is full of things on this photograph. But the room that we were in didn't have this square window; instead, there was a round opening that probably was used for ventilation purposes before, but it was blocked up with rags. So we were staying in a room that was identical to this one, regarding the walls and everything else except the window. There was just concrete on the floor and nothing inside except for the three benches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please put your name on the photograph and today's date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the photograph with the number 89, can we have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P45. Next photograph, please, the last digits being 88. Does this photograph and the door shown on it, is it the entrance door through which you went to enter the room you were held in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is 100 per cent that door. That is the outside of the room viewed from the door -- from the road, I'm sorry. Yes. There was only that one door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about the window at the bottom of the photograph? That is not the window that existed when you were there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it didn't. There wasn't any window of that shape and size. So roughly, instead there was this opening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this window have been put there later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably, but I must say that at the time it did not exist. That, I can claim with certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the opening that you mentioned, was it in the place where the window is on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, roughly on that same wall, that is, the black wall of that room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Put your first and last name on the photograph and today's date, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can I have an exhibit number for this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P46. No more photographs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: One more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another one. I see, 87. The photograph with the last digits being 87, this photograph was the first that was shown to you, and you told us in response to a question from the Prosecution that this was the door you entered through when you were taken to the room in which you were detained; and that this photograph showed what you called the blacksmith's shop. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is the entrance door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You will note that on this door, at the bottom there's a cement slanting piece. Do you remember this piece that is shown on the photograph, leading up to the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember 100 per cent whether it looked quite like this, the area in front of the door. But I don't remember there being any step. It was on a same level as the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Above the door, there seems to be an iron -- a small iron roof. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember whether it was there or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't remember; I see. He doesn't remember the roof, nor the slanting piece of cement leading to the door. Put your name on the photograph and today's date, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we have an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. exhibit number for this photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P47. The Prosecution, you have the floor again to continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, may I state that these pictures were taken in the year 2002. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can you also tell us the month when these photos were taken? Do you know the date -- the day and the month? Mr. Withopf, maybe you can give us more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, Your Honours, since my colleague at the time wasn't part of the trial team yet, I can provide you with the information necessary. If my recollection is not completely wrong, this photograph was taken in April 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Madam Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, now that we have described the physical appearance of the room, could you describe the conditions that operated at the time while you were confined to that room. Could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: The conditions were terrible. At the very beginning of our detention, there were some 10 or 11 of us in that room. After the general attack, some other people were brought in and detained together with us. There were three benches inside. Only a few people could sit on them. There was nothing to sleep on. There was also a black plastic bucket that we used to relieve ourselves in. That was at the beginning. Later on they started to take us out to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: During this period of confinement, could you tell the Trial Chamber were you fed? How was your eating?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, for the first three or four days we did not receive any food or water. It was only after three or four days that they would start bringing us three or four tins a day and a loaf of bread. But all this was terrible. This was not food, nothing to speak of.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: During your confinement, were you personally subjected to any form of interrogation at any time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, two days after our arrest, when the general attack took place, when the other Croatian villages were attacked and the population expelled from them, some three or four days later some other people joined us. The school had been full of Croat civilians, women, children, some elderly people as well. After that, some 15 days later there was an exchange. The civilians went towards Nova Bila, where they were exchanged --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, excuse me for one moment, for interrupting. But at this point in time, could I ask you to tell the Court during your confinement in the shop if you were ever subjected to any questioning of any sort. That's the question. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I was interrogated. But I just wanted to follow a certain order. They did take us out to that building for interrogation. That's where the Ugar restaurant was. Two men in military uniforms with white belts waited for us there, and we were taken for interrogation one by one. These two men came. And this lasted for two or three days. So these two young men were there for the two or three days, and they waited for us and they interrogated us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Were you subject to any mistreatment at all during your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: There were all sorts of ill-treatment during interrogation. They introduced to -- themselves to us as military policemen from Zenica. They were my age. One of them was interrogating us and the other was on the other side of the desk. He had a knife in his hand. He was threatening us. They were interrogating us about Croatian units, the HVO. They asked us about some movements that we didn't have a clue about. We didn't know why we were detained and why we were subjected to such conditions, why we were put in this place.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And these men who described themselves as military policemen, were you able to identify if they came from any particular battalion?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: They introduced themselves as military police from Zenica. They had white belts and pistols. I can't remember their names. I had never seen them before, and I never saw them after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any injured persons in your group in the blacksmith's shop with you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: Once we were joined by some other people, on the 8th of June, after the general attack. Zeljko Puselja came. He was wounded in one of his arms. I don't remember which one. His arm was fractured and the wound had never been treated properly. He was heavily wounded. He had escaped the execution site in Bikose a few days earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. During your trips to the other buildings, tell the Trial Chamber if you were able to observe anything about these buildings, the occupants, you know, what the building looked like. Could you assist the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: Once the civilians were exchanged, once our civilians, women, children, and elderly people left, they took us up there to clean some sewage pipes around the school. We did that for two days. And while we were doing that, we noticed a number of soldiers around the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you describe in detail for us if you at that time was able to recognise what battalion these soldiers may have been from, or who they were.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: I did not dare stare too much, but on the third floor of the school we noticed Mujahedin units. They wore arms. They had short beards. And their -- the colour of their skin was somewhat darker. They were on the third floor of the school. On the second floor of the school, there was also a number of troops. Allegedly they had come from Krajina. And also, there was the 7th Muslim unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Continue. Were you ...?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: And on the first floor, there was also an army, the BH Army, as they called it at that time. In any case, there were troops on all three floors. They humiliated us; they insulted us. While we were on the cleaning detail, they humiliated us and they were supposed just to guard us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: For how long did you remain at the blacksmith's shop?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: I stayed for about a month in that room, until the moment I was transferred to another prison, the KP Dom in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And, Witness, finally, from the KP Dom could you tell us where you were transferred to or what happened.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: After my transfer from the KP Dom, there was an exchange. We didn't know anything about the exchange. They just put us on buses, and we were exchanged in the area of Zepce.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And when you got to Zepce, did you join any army, any particular army?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Zepce some 10 or 15 days later, I joined an HVO unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Finally, Witness, for this Trial Chamber could you tell us how you feel now with respect to your experience in that period of June 1993. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: To be honest, I'm trying to forget and leave all that behind. It is impossible though. It has left -- it has made an impact on my mental health, on my physical condition. I'm a 70-per cent-disabled person, but what can I do?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: During that period, did you lose weight or did you maintain your weight? Could you tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: During my stay in the KP Dom Zenica, the conditions were terrible, the food was poor. And when I arrived in Zepce, I had lost 26 kilos. There were some other people though who were on the very brink of survival.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Benjamin. Before I give the floor to the Defence, I have some questions to ask you in order to clarify things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were arrested, what was your status? Were you a civilian or were you a soldier? Were you a member of the HVO at the time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO TADIC
utterances.text: When I was arrested, I was arrested as a civilian. I was a shepherd. I was guarding sheep. However, the units that captured us, judging by their treatment during the arrest and during my detention, they treated us as soldiers, HVO soldiers; although we were not HVO soldiers.
